fullCitation: Mawji A, Li E, Dunsmuir D, Komugisha C, Novakowski SK, Wiens MO, Vesuvius TA, Kissoon N, Ansermino JM. Smart triage: Development of a rapid pediatric triage algorithm for use in low-and-middle income countries. Frontiers in Pediatrics. 2022 Nov 22;10:976870. doi:10.3389/fped.2022.976870. — External validation: Kigo J, Kamau G, et al. External validation of a paediatric Smart Triage model for use in resource limited facilities. PLOS Digital Health. 2024 Jun;3(6):e0000293. doi:10.1371/journal.pdig.0000293.
laySummary: Health clinics in poor countries are often overwhelmed with sick children, and there aren't enough trained staff to spot which child is dangerously ill and needs care first. This team built "Smart Triage": a tablet app plus a clip-on finger sensor that a nurse uses at the front door of the clinic. In under a few minutes it collects a few simple facts (the child's age, whether the parent is worried, whether the child has trouble breathing, swelling, or paleness) together with automatically measured vital signs (heart rate, oxygen level, temperature, arm thickness). A simple statistical formula then scores the child and sorts them into red (emergency), yellow (priority), or green (non-urgent). Built from about 1,600 children in Uganda and later tested on about 5,000 children in Kenya, the tool reliably flagged the children who ended up needing hospital admission (accuracy score around 0.82 out of 1), so scarce staff can focus on the sickest children first.
dataset: Development ("derivation") data came from a prospective cohort study: acutely ill children (roughly under 5 years old, the WHO under-five triage population) presenting to the emergency/outpatient department of Jinja Regional Referral Hospital in Eastern Uganda. The derivation cohort was 1,612 participants, with a hospital-admission rate of about 23%. The prediction TARGET (the label the model learns to predict) was hospital admission, used as an objective proxy for "critically ill / needs urgent care" — each child's admission outcome was recorded by clinical staff. Data were collected prospectively via the tablet app (not retrospective chart review). The data are not a public/open dataset (private, held by the BC Children's Hospital / partner sites). Model performance was assessed on a held-out test set created by an 80:20 train/test split with 10-fold cross-validation on the training portion. The external validation (Kigo et al., PLOS Digital Health 2024) used two Kenyan hospitals: 2,539 eligible children at Hospital 1 and 2,464 at Hospital 2 (5,003 combined), again predicting hospital admission.
device: The device is a consumer Android tablet — specifically a Samsung Galaxy A8 — running a custom, password-protected data-collection/triage app built by the research team; a separate clinician dashboard runs on a laptop or tablet. It is NOT "any ordinary phone runs it": a dedicated custom app is required, and the measurement setup needs an add-on sensor. The vital-sign hardware is a Masimo iSpO2 clip-on fingertip pulse oximeter that plugs into the tablet (a genuine optical clip sensor, not a phone-camera trick). Respiratory rate uses a software module (RRate) built into the app — no extra hardware. Rough cost: the Samsung Galaxy A8 tablet is ~US$200-250 and the Masimo iSpO2 is a commercial medical-grade accessory at roughly US$200-300, so the combined kit is well ABOVE the NT$5,000 (~US$155) threshold — this is a clip-on medical oximeter, not a sub-US$155 gadget. A dedicated app is required (Android). The app/algorithm are NOT released as open source — no public code repository for the Smart Triage tablet app was found (the reusable part is the published 9-variable logistic equation, which anyone can re-implement; the RRate respiratory-rate method is separately published by the same lab).
vitalsAndSensing: Heart rate (HR): read directly from the Masimo iSpO2 clip-on fingertip sensor connected to the tablet. Oxygen saturation (SpO2): also from the Masimo iSpO2 clip — a true optical pulse oximeter that shines red/infrared light through the fingertip and measures how much is absorbed by oxygen-carrying blood; the tablet app logs the value (the model uses a mathematically "transformed" SpO2). Respiratory rate: measured with RRate, a tap-along module built into the Android app — the user taps the screen with each breath the child takes and the software converts the tapping rhythm into breaths-per-minute (note: RR was collected but did NOT make it into the final 9-predictor model). Temperature: measured with a thermometer and entered/recorded by the nurse in the app. Mid-upper-arm circumference (MUAC): measured with a MUAC tape (a proxy for nutritional status) and entered in the app. Blood pressure was not part of the model. Additional observed clinical signs (oedema/swelling, pallor/paleness) are recorded by the nurse via the app.
chiefComplaintUse: Symptoms and danger signs are captured as a short structured questionnaire/checklist on the tablet, filled in by the study nurse — not free text. The clinically relevant items that survived feature selection into the model are: "parental/caregiver concern" (a yes/no — is the parent worried the child is very sick), "difficulty breathing," and the observed signs "oedema" and "pallor." These caregiver-reported symptoms and WHO-style danger signs are then combined arithmetically with the measured vitals (age, heart rate, temperature, MUAC, transformed SpO2) inside a single logistic-regression formula that outputs one admission-risk probability. So symptoms and vitals are not scored separately — they are weighted terms in the same equation.
pipelineDetail: Child arrives at triage: an acutely ill child and caregiver present at the clinic's outpatient/emergency entrance. Nurse enters symptoms & danger signs: on the tablet app the nurse records caregiver concern, difficulty breathing, and observed oedema and pallor. Clip-on oximeter reads SpO2 & HR: the Masimo iSpO2 finger sensor plugged into the tablet automatically captures oxygen saturation and heart rate. Measure temperature, MUAC, resp rate: a thermometer gives temperature, a MUAC tape gives arm circumference, and the in-app RRate tap tool estimates breaths per minute. Compute 9-feature risk score: the logistic-regression equation combines square-root of age, heart rate, temperature, MUAC, transformed SpO2, caregiver concern, difficulty breathing, oedema and pallor into one admission-probability between 0 and 1. Apply 8% & 40% thresholds: the probability is compared against a low cut-off (8%) tuned for ~90% sensitivity and a high cut-off (40%) tuned for ~90% specificity. Assign emergency/priority/non-urgent: probability at/above 40% = emergency (red), 8-40% = priority (yellow), below 8% = non-urgent (green). Show on dashboard & track patient: the risk category and a Bluetooth patient-tracking tag feed a clinician dashboard that lists highest-risk children first.
submodules: 1) Triage risk model — the core trained component: a multivariable LOGISTIC REGRESSION predicting hospital admission. Feature selection used bootstrap stepwise regression, reducing many candidate variables to 9 predictors. Fit on the Jinja, Uganda derivation cohort (n=1,612). Inputs: sqrt(age), heart rate, temperature, MUAC, transformed SpO2, parental concern, difficulty breathing, oedema, pallor. Output: admission probability (0-1). Published coefficients: logit(p) = -32.888 + 0.252·sqrt(age) + 0.016·HR + 0.819·temperature - 0.022·MUAC + 0.048·transformedSpO2 + 1.793·parentConcern + 1.012·difficultyBreathing + 1.814·oedema + 1.506·pallor. 2) Threshold/risk-stratification rule — not a learned model but a fitted decision layer: the 8% and 40% cut-offs were chosen on the data to hit ~90% sensitivity (low cut) and ~90% specificity (high cut). 3) RRate respiratory-rate estimator — a signal-processing/tap-timing algorithm in the app converting screen taps to breaths/min (separate published method, not part of the 9-predictor model). 4) SpO2/HR — produced by the Masimo iSpO2 hardware's onboard pulse-oximetry processing, not trained by this team. External recalibration (Kigo 2024) re-fit only the model intercept to the Kenyan sites.
keyResults: Derivation/internal validation (Uganda): the 9-predictor logistic model showed good discrimination, calibration and risk stratification at the chosen 8% and 40% probability thresholds; the low threshold was set for ~90% minimum sensitivity and the high threshold for ~90% specificity, producing the three-tier emergency/priority/non-urgent split. External validation (Kenya, Kigo et al. 2024, n=5,003 across two hospitals): area under the ROC curve (a 0.5=chance, 1.0=perfect accuracy score for ranking who gets admitted) was 0.826 at Hospital 1, 0.784 at Hospital 2, and 0.821 combined — i.e. good, transportable discrimination. Admission rates in the validation sites were 8.9%, 4.5% and 6.8%. Calibration required recalibrating the model intercept for the new setting. Real-world implementation reports (companion papers) noted operational gains such as time to IV antimicrobial administration falling ~57% in Kenya.
limitations: Outcome is a proxy: the model predicts hospital ADMISSION, which is a stand-in for "critically ill / needs urgent care" and can be influenced by non-clinical admission practices, so it is not a direct measure of severity. Single-site derivation (one Ugandan hospital) limits generalisability; external validation needed intercept recalibration to work in Kenya, showing the raw model does not transfer perfectly. Respiratory rate, though collected, was dropped from the final model. MUAC/temperature depend on correct manual measurement and app entry. The tool identifies risk but does not diagnose a specific disease. Requires a specific tablet app and a commercial clip-on oximeter, so it is not runnable on any ordinary phone and the kit exceeds a low-cost (<US$155) budget. Model built on under-fives and found less suitable for neonates in later age-group validation.
glossary: Triage: sorting patients by how urgently they need care. AUROC/AUC: a 0.5-1.0 score for how well a model ranks sicker vs less-sick patients (higher is better). Sensitivity: share of truly sick children the tool correctly flags. Specificity: share of not-sick children it correctly clears. Logistic regression: a statistical formula that weighs several inputs and outputs a probability between 0 and 1. Feature/predictor: one input variable used by the model. Bootstrap stepwise regression: a method that repeatedly resamples the data to pick the most reliably useful predictors. Calibration: whether predicted probabilities match real-world rates. SpO2: blood oxygen saturation (%). Pulse oximeter: a finger clip that measures SpO2 and heart rate with light. MUAC: mid-upper-arm circumference, a quick nutrition/illness indicator. Oedema: swelling from fluid. Pallor: paleness (often anaemia). WHO danger signs: warning signs (e.g. difficulty breathing) the WHO uses to flag serious childhood illness. LMIC: low- and middle-income country.
clinicalProblem: In low- and middle-income country clinics, large numbers of sick children arrive at crowded outpatient/emergency departments with too few trained staff to quickly tell which child is critically ill (including early sepsis). Delays in spotting the sickest children cost lives. The problem is to give frontline workers a fast, low-training way to reliably sort children into who needs care now versus who can safely wait — at the very first point of contact.
sensors: Masimo iSpO2 pulse oximeter: a clip that goes on the child's fingertip and connects to the tablet. It works by shining two wavelengths of light (red and infrared) through the finger; oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood absorb these colours differently, and the pulsing of blood with each heartbeat lets the sensor calculate both oxygen saturation (SpO2) and heart rate. RRate (software "sensor"): uses the tablet touchscreen — the operator taps once per breath and the algorithm turns the tap intervals into a respiratory rate. Thermometer: standard temperature probe, value entered in the app. MUAC tape: a paper/plastic measuring tape wrapped around the upper arm to gauge nutritional status. The nurse-observed signs (oedema, pallor, difficulty breathing, caregiver concern) are "human sensors" entered as checklist answers.
citationCount: Exact count could not be confirmed — the Semantic Scholar and Google Scholar pages were inaccessible through the research proxy (all publisher/scholar fetches returned 403). The paper (Frontiers in Pediatrics, Nov 2022) has a Semantic Scholar record and is cited by numerous follow-on Smart Triage papers (external validation, geographical validation, cost-effectiveness, implementation studies); a reasonable estimate is on the order of several dozen citations (~40-90) as of 2026, but treat this as unverified.
impactFactor: Frontiers in Pediatrics: approximately 3.4 Journal Impact Factor for 2021 and CiteScore ~3.2, Q1 in Pediatrics (source: journalsearches.com / Researcher.Life aggregations of Clarivate JCR and Scopus). The 2022 JCR value is commonly reported lower (~2.6). Figures are from third-party aggregators, not read directly from Clarivate, so treat the exact number as approximate.
confidenceNotes: I could NOT open the primary full texts directly: the egress proxy returned 403 for Frontiers, PMC, PLOS, medRxiv, ResearchGate, Semantic Scholar and the Jina reader, and blocked Crossref/OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar APIs. All figures were therefore assembled from detailed WebSearch result summaries of those same sources, which quoted specific numbers (n=1,612; ~23% admission; the exact 9-predictor logistic equation and coefficients; 8%/40% thresholds; validation n=5,003 and AUROC 0.826/0.784/0.821; Samsung Galaxy A8 + Masimo iSpO2 + RRate). IMPORTANT DISCREPANCY WITH THE TASK PROMPT: the task described the model as "XGBoost / feature-selected," but the actual published Smart Triage derivation used LOGISTIC REGRESSION with bootstrap stepwise feature selection, not XGBoost — I went with the paper. Device cost figures are market estimates, not stated retail prices from the paper. Citation count and the precise journal impact factor/year are unverified (see those fields). Whether any Smart Triage app source code is public could not be confirmed; no official repository was found.

fullCitation: Lim J, Cloete G, Dunsmuir DT, Payne BA, Scheffer C, von Dadelszen P, Dumont GA, Ansermino JM. Usability and Feasibility of PIERS on the Move: An mHealth App for Pre-Eclampsia Triage. JMIR mHealth and uHealth. 2015 Apr 29;3(2):e37. doi:10.2196/mhealth.3942. PMID 25887292; PMCID PMC4417132. (Underlying model: Payne BA, Hutcheon JA, Ansermino JM, et al. A Risk Prediction Model for the Assessment and Triage of Women with Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy in Low-Resourced Settings: The miniPIERS Multi-country Prospective Cohort Study. PLoS Medicine. 2014;11(1):e1001589. doi:10.1371/journal.pmed.1001589.)
clinicalProblem: Pre-eclampsia and related hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are a leading cause of maternal death, and the great majority of those deaths happen in low- and middle-income countries where there are few doctors, little lab access, and long distances to hospitals. A frontline nurse, midwife or community health worker at a clinic often cannot easily tell which pregnant woman with high blood pressure is about to become critically ill (seizures, organ failure, death within a day or two) and therefore needs urgent referral, versus who can be safely managed locally. The paper describes and tests a low-cost smartphone tool, "PIERS on the Move" (PotM), that guides such a worker through collecting a few symptoms and measurements — including blood oxygen saturation via a clip-on finger sensor plugged into the phone — and then computes a risk score to help decide who to refer. The patients are pregnant women (typically 20+ weeks gestation) presenting with, or being screened for, hypertension in resource-poor settings in Africa and South Asia.
laySummary: Pre-eclampsia (dangerously high blood pressure in pregnancy) kills many women in poor countries where clinics lack doctors and lab tests. The researchers built a cheap smartphone app called "PIERS on the Move" that a nurse or health worker uses at the bedside: it asks a short checklist of symptoms, records blood pressure and a urine dipstick result, and reads blood-oxygen level from a small clip that plugs into the phone and shines light through the fingertip. The app feeds these into an existing statistical risk model (miniPIERS) that estimates the chance the woman will suffer a severe complication within 48 hours, and shows a triage recommendation. In testing with 37 South African nurses and midwives the app was found usable after design fixes, and in a pilot one nurse completed 500+ assessments on 200+ patients, each taking about 5 minutes. The study shows the tool is feasible and usable, but it did not prove it improves patient outcomes.
dataset: Two distinct data sources matter here. (A) The PotM usability/feasibility study itself (this paper) was not a machine-learning training study — it was a human-factors and field-feasibility evaluation. Usability: 37 nurses and midwives in South Africa evaluated the interface (a reported 22 of them at Frere Maternity Hospital, East London), completing scripted clinical-scenario tasks while thinking aloud, across two iterative design rounds. Feasibility: one research nurse used PotM in a pilot clinical deployment, performing more than 500 evaluations on more than 200 pregnant patients. No diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity/specificity) of PotM against outcomes was reported in this paper; endpoints were usability metrics and time-to-complete. (B) The embedded risk model, miniPIERS, was developed separately (Payne et al., PLoS Medicine 2014) on a prospective multi-country cohort of 2,081 women admitted with any hypertensive disorder of pregnancy, collected 1 July 2008 – 31 March 2012 at sites in five low- and middle-income countries (including South Africa, Pakistan, Fiji and Brazil). The prediction target/label was a composite adverse maternal outcome (maternal death or a specified serious end-organ complication) within 48 hours of admission; labels came from prospective clinical follow-up. Development used internal validation (bootstrap); it was a prospectively collected, initially private research dataset.
device: The platform is an off-the-shelf Android smartphone running the dedicated PotM app, paired with an external clip-on/finger pulse-oximeter probe — the "Phone Oximeter" developed at the University of British Columbia and commercialised by LionsGate Technologies (LGTmedical). Critically, SpO2 is NOT read from the phone's camera; it comes from a genuine medical oximeter sensor (Nonin-type probe/Xpod-class module) that connects to the phone (early Phone Oximeter versions interfaced through the audio/headset jack, which is what allowed ordinary low-cost phones to be used). So the phone itself needs no special hardware — any reasonable Android handset works — but the system does require the add-on oximeter probe; it is not a camera-only, any-phone solution. Cost: the oximeter attachment was targeted at roughly US$40, and a mid-range Android phone is similarly inexpensive, so the full kit sits well under NT$5000 (~US$155). A dedicated Android app is required (the miniPIERS logic and oximeter integration are built in; it is not a generic form). The app and its source code are NOT open source — it is proprietary research/commercial software (UBC / CFRI / LGTmedical); no public code repository was found. Reported field issues included the oximeter attachment connection being fragile and phone battery life over a full day of community visits.
vitalsAndSensing: Signs captured: (1) Blood oxygen saturation (SpO2) and pulse rate — sensed by the clip-on Phone Oximeter probe, not by the phone. The probe places the fingertip between a light source and a detector; it shines red and infrared light through the finger and measures how much each colour is absorbed. Oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood absorb the two wavelengths differently, and the pulsing (arterial) portion of the signal is isolated so the oximeter's algorithm can compute the percentage of haemoglobin carrying oxygen (SpO2) plus heart rate; the value is passed to the phone app. (2) Blood pressure (systolic, and diastolic) — measured with a standard BP cuff/device and typed into the app by the worker (not auto-sensed). (3) Urine protein — read from a standard urine dipstick and entered as a category. (4) Symptoms and history — entered by the worker via checklists/fields (see next). So only SpO2/pulse are instrument-sensed by the attached device; BP and dipstick are conventional measurements manually entered.
chiefComplaintUse: Symptoms are captured as a structured checklist / discrete entry fields rather than free text, matching the predictor set of the miniPIERS model: the worker records danger-sign symptoms — headache and/or visual disturbances, chest pain and/or shortness of breath (dyspnoea), and vaginal bleeding with abdominal pain — plus history items such as parity (first pregnancy vs. later) and gestational age. These symptom flags are combined in the app with the measured/entered clinical signs (systolic blood pressure, dipstick proteinuria) and the sensor-derived SpO2. All of these are fed together into the miniPIERS logistic-regression equation, which returns a single predicted probability of a severe adverse maternal outcome; the app converts that into a triage/risk display for the worker. So the symptoms are not used in isolation — they are inputs to the same risk calculation as the vitals.
pipelineDetail: Enter symptoms & history: the worker taps through a guided checklist recording danger-sign symptoms (headache/visual changes, chest pain/breathlessness, vaginal bleeding with abdominal pain), parity and gestational age. Enter blood pressure: systolic (and diastolic) blood pressure from a standard cuff is typed in. Enter urine dipstick: the protein level from a standard urine dipstick is selected as a category. Measure SpO2 (Phone Oximeter): the finger probe plugged into the phone shines red/infrared light through the fingertip and returns blood-oxygen saturation and pulse into the app. miniPIERS risk calculation: a pre-trained logistic-regression equation combines these inputs into a single predicted probability of a severe maternal complication within 48 hours. Show risk / triage output: the app displays the resulting risk level (e.g. a colour-coded/traffic-light style category) to the worker. Referral & management guidance: based on that risk level the app supports the decision to keep, treat, or urgently refer the woman.
submodules: miniPIERS risk model — the only trained/statistical component. Role: convert symptoms + signs + SpO2 into a probability of a composite adverse maternal outcome (death or major end-organ complication) within 48 hours, for triage. Algorithm: multivariable logistic regression built by step-wise backward elimination. Trained/fit on: 2,081 women with hypertensive disorders of pregnancy across five low-/middle-income-country sites (Payne et al., PLoS Medicine 2014), with predictors collected within 24 h of admission and outcomes ascertained prospectively; internally validated by bootstrap. Inputs: parity, gestational age at assessment, headache/visual disturbances, chest pain/dyspnoea, vaginal bleeding with abdominal pain, systolic blood pressure, dipstick proteinuria — and, in the PotM/extended version, added peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2). Output: a continuous predicted risk probability, thresholded into triage categories. Note: the oximeter's SpO2 computation is a signal-processing algorithm (red/infrared absorption ratio), not a learned model, so it is a device sub-component rather than a trained ML module; PotM's usability/feasibility paper did not train any new model.
keyResults: This paper's endpoints were usability and feasibility, not diagnostic accuracy. Usability (iterative, two rounds): Study 1 surfaced major problems with the touch keyboard and date scroll-wheels (total errors n=212); Study 2, after redesign, focused on navigation improvements (total errors n=144). On the Computer Systems Usability Questionnaire (1–7, lower=better) median scores improved from 2 (range 1–6) in Study 1 to 1 (range 1–7) in Study 2, i.e. users judged it usable. Feasibility: one research nurse completed 500+ evaluations on 200+ patients; median time per full evaluation was 4 min 55 sec (range 3:25–6:56). For the embedded model's performance (from the separate miniPIERS paper): AUC/area-under-ROC = 0.768 (95% CI 0.735–0.801) for the 48-hour adverse-outcome prediction, with good calibration. A related analysis (Payne et al., JOGC) showed adding SpO2 to miniPIERS raised sensitivity from ~32.8% to ~49.6% at only a small specificity cost (~96.2% to ~91.5%), which is the rationale for including the Phone Oximeter.
limitations: (1) This was a usability/feasibility study, not a clinical-outcomes trial — it did not demonstrate that PotM improves maternal outcomes, reduces deaths, or that its triage decisions are accurate in the field. (2) Small, single-country evaluation (37 nurses/midwives in South Africa) and a feasibility pilot run by a single research nurse, limiting generalisability. (3) Practical hardware problems were noted: fragile/poor connection of the oximeter attachment and inadequate phone battery life over a full day of community visits. (4) The tool depends on an external oximeter probe and manual entry of BP and dipstick, so data quality relies on the worker and on functioning peripherals. (5) The underlying miniPIERS model has only moderate discrimination (AUC ~0.77) and modest sensitivity, and was developed on a specific cohort, so calibration/performance in new populations is uncertain. (6) The app/code is proprietary and not open source, limiting external scrutiny and reuse.
citationCount: Approximately 60 citing works listed on the JMIR/Crossref citation page for the article (mhealth.jmir.org/2015/2/e37/citations), as surfaced via web search circa 2024–2025. I could not directly load Google Scholar or Semantic Scholar (both blocked by the session's egress proxy), so the precise Google Scholar count is unconfirmed; treat ~60 (Crossref-linked) as a lower-bound estimate.
impactFactor: JMIR mHealth and uHealth: Journal Impact Factor 5.4 (2024 JCR, Clarivate); CiteScore 2024 = 11.6 (Scopus), Q1 in Health Informatics (~#13/153, 91st percentile). Note these are current metrics; the journal did not have a mature JIF at the 2015 publication date.
glossary: Pre-eclampsia: a pregnancy complication of high blood pressure plus signs of organ stress, dangerous to mother and baby. Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy: umbrella term for high-blood-pressure conditions in pregnancy, including pre-eclampsia. Triage: quickly sorting patients by how urgently they need care. SpO2 / pulse oximetry: percentage of blood haemoglobin carrying oxygen, measured by shining light through a fingertip. Pulse oximeter probe: the clip/sensor that does that light measurement. mHealth: healthcare delivered via mobile phones. miniPIERS: the specific risk-prediction model (Pre-eclampsia Integrated Estimate of RiSk, minimal version) used inside the app. Logistic regression: a statistical model that weights several inputs to output a probability. AUC / ROC: a 0.5–1.0 score of how well a model separates high-risk from low-risk (1.0 = perfect). Sensitivity: share of truly high-risk patients the model correctly flags. Specificity: share of low-risk patients correctly cleared. Calibration: whether predicted probabilities match observed frequencies. Parity: number of previous births. Gestational age: how far along the pregnancy is. Proteinuria: protein in the urine, a pre-eclampsia sign. Dyspnoea: shortness of breath. SUS/CSUQ: standardised questionnaires scoring how usable software is.
confidenceNotes: Could not open the full text directly: JMIR, PMC, Europe PMC, ResearchGate, DOI resolver, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar were all blocked by the session's egress proxy (HTTP 403 on WebFetch and curl). All detail was reconstructed from WebSearch result snippets of the article and its abstract, the miniPIERS PLoS Medicine paper, and the JOGC SpO2 paper — high-confidence for the numbers quoted verbatim in those snippets. (2) The precise numeric risk threshold / colour-coding scheme the app used to convert probability into a triage category — described generically. (3) Whether SpO2 is formally part of the deployed PotM model equation vs. displayed alongside — miniPIERS's published 7-variable model did NOT include SpO2, but PotM integrates the oximeter and the team's follow-up work added SpO2; I flag this as the one place to verify against full text. (4) Exact split of the 37 usability participants and precise CSUQ scoring direction. (5) Citation count is an estimate (~60, Crossref-linked) not a confirmed Google Scholar figure. Journal IF/CiteScore are current (2024) values, correctly noted as post-dating the 2015 publication.

fullCitation: Raposo A, Marques L, Correia R, Melo F, Valente J, Pereira T, Rosário LB, Froes F, Sanches J, Plácido da Silva H. e-CoVig: A Novel mHealth System for Remote Monitoring of Symptoms in COVID-19. Sensors. 2021;21(10):3397. doi:10.3390/s21103397.
laySummary: During COVID-19, patients isolating at home were followed up mostly by nurses phoning them, which was slow and gave doctors no hard numbers. This team from Lisbon built e-CoVig: a free smartphone app plus an optional cheap plug-in gadget that lets a patient measure their own fever, blood-oxygen level, heart rate, and record their cough and breathing, and answer a symptom checklist — all sent automatically to a hospital web dashboard. The idea is that clinicians can watch many patients at once and quickly spot the ones getting worse, instead of relying on a phone call. The paper is an engineering "here is the system we built and got working" report rather than a clinical trial: it describes the hardware, the app, and the cloud, and shows the signals can be captured, but it does not train a diagnostic AI or report accuracy against COVID outcomes.
dataset: This is a system-engineering / proof-of-concept paper, not a machine-learning study, so it has no large labelled training dataset and no train/test split. The work was done in Portugal (Instituto Superior Técnico and Instituto de Telecomunicações, Lisbon, with clinical input from pulmonologists Filipe Froes and Luís Brás Rosário linked to Lisbon hospitals). Validation was technical/feasibility demonstration on the authors' own prototype — e.g. showing that the purpose-built device and the phone-camera method both produce usable PPG/vital-sign signals and that the OCR reads device displays — rather than a prospective clinical cohort with COVID-positive/negative labels. No patient sample size (n), no diagnostic ground-truth labels, and no public dataset are reported. CONFIDENCE: I could not open the full PDF (publisher, ResearchGate, PMC and Semantic Scholar were all blocked by the session egress policy); if the paper reports a small pilot count of test acquisitions, I could not confirm it.
device: Primary interface is an ordinary consumer smartphone running a dedicated app built with Flutter and tested on Android (a public listing exists as "e-CoVig" on Google Play, package com.ecovig.app). Any reasonably modern phone with a rear camera + flash and a microphone can run the software-only functions (camera-based PPG/heart rate, audio capture of cough/breathing, and OCR reading of household device displays), so no special phone model is mandated. For higher-quality temperature and SpO2 the team also built an OPTIONAL low-cost, low-power add-on device: an Espressif ESP32 microcontroller (single-core 32-bit @160 MHz, 520 KiB SRAM, integrated Wi-Fi + Bluetooth/BLE) coupled to a Maxim MAX30101 optical pulse-oximeter/heart-rate sensor driven by a MAX32664 biometric sensor hub, plus a Melexis MLX90614 non-contact infrared thermometer. These parts are individually cheap (ESP32 a few US$, MAX30101 ~US$5-10, MLX90614 ~US$5-15), so the bill of materials is on the order of tens of US$ — comfortably under NT$5000 (~US$155); the exact total cost was not confirmed from the full text and is my estimate. A dedicated app IS required. Open source: the phone-camera PPG component is openly published by the first author on GitHub (github.com/Afonsocraposo/ppg, Flutter/Android); I could not confirm that the complete e-CoVig app, firmware, and cloud stack are released under an open licence.
vitalsAndSensing: Body temperature: measured with a Melexis MLX90614 non-contact infrared thermometer — it senses the infrared heat radiating from a surface, so pointing it at the forehead skin or into the ear (tympanic) gives body temperature without touching; alternatively the phone camera reads the number off a household thermometer's digital display via OCR. Blood-oxygen saturation (SpO2) and heart rate: measured with the MAX30101 optical sensor (via the MAX32664 hub) — it shines red and infrared LEDs into a fingertip and measures how much light the pulsing blood absorbs; because oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood absorb red vs infrared light differently, the ratio yields SpO2, and the pulsation gives heart rate. Photoplethysmography (PPG)/heart rate can ALSO be obtained software-only by placing a fingertip over the phone's rear camera with the flash on: the camera films tiny colour/brightness changes as blood pulses through the finger, and signal processing extracts the pulse waveform and rate. Cough and respiration: recorded as audio using the phone's built-in microphone. Self-reported symptoms are entered by the patient. Note: robust SpO2 needs the dedicated MAX30101 device (or OCR of a real oximeter); the plain phone camera reliably gives PPG/heart rate but the paper does not claim clinical-grade SpO2 from the camera alone.
chiefComplaintUse: Symptoms are captured as patient-facing self-report questionnaires inside the app, covering COVID-19 symptomatology and other clinically relevant items (structured checklist-style entries rather than free text alone). These subjective reports are transmitted alongside the objective measured vitals (temperature, SpO2, heart rate, cough/breath audio) and shown together on the clinician web dashboard, so a human clinician — not an automated score — combines the symptom answers with the numbers to judge severity and decide who needs attention. The paper does not describe an automated triage/danger-sign algorithm that fuses symptoms and vitals into an acuity score; the fusion is done by the reviewing health professional.
pipelineDetail: Patient self-reports symptoms: the patient fills a COVID-19 symptom questionnaire in the app. Measure temperature: the MLX90614 infrared sensor (or the phone camera reading a thermometer) captures body temperature. Measure SpO2 / heart rate: the MAX30101 finger sensor, or the phone camera pressed by a fingertip, records the pulsing-blood (PPG) signal from which oxygen saturation and heart rate are derived. Record cough & breath audio: the phone microphone captures cough and respiration sounds for later characterisation. OCR reads device display: when a household oximeter or thermometer is used, the phone camera photographs its digital screen and an optical-character-recognition model reads the numbers automatically. Encrypt & upload to cloud: the app packages symptoms, vitals and audio and sends them securely to the web/cloud e-Health platform. Clinician dashboard review: doctors and nurses view each patient's aggregated data over time on the web platform. Triage / deterioration flag: the clinician spots worsening patients and prioritises follow-up or escalation.
submodules: OCR display reader: role is to turn a photo of a commercial oximeter/thermometer's digital display into a numeric value; implemented with an optical-character-recognition engine (a pretrained text-recognition model bundled via the mobile toolchain, e.g. an ML-Kit/Tesseract-style recognizer — the paper does not report training its own OCR model). Camera-PPG signal processing: role is to extract a pulse waveform and heart rate from the fingertip-on-camera video; this is classical signal processing (frame-brightness time series, filtering, peak detection), not a trained neural network, and is published as open source (Afonsocraposo/ppg). Device SpO2/HR estimation: performed largely on the MAX30101 + MAX32664 sensor-hub firmware, which computes SpO2 and heart rate from the red/infrared PPG using the manufacturer's onboard algorithm rather than a model trained by the authors. Cough/respiration audio: captured and transmitted for clinical/expert characterisation; the paper does NOT report a trained cough classifier. Overall, e-CoVig contains no bespoke author-trained diagnostic ML model — the only learned component is the off-the-shelf OCR recognizer.
keyResults: Because e-CoVig is a system/feasibility paper, it reports demonstrated functionality rather than diagnostic accuracy metrics. Reported achievements: a working end-to-end pipeline (app + cloud dashboard + low-cost ESP32/MAX30101/MLX90614 device); successful acquisition of temperature, SpO2, heart rate and PPG both from the dedicated device and from an ordinary phone; working camera-based PPG/heart-rate estimation; audio capture of cough/respiration; and a functioning OCR feature that reads temperature/SpO2 off commercial device displays so patients can reuse gadgets they already own. No AUC, sensitivity/specificity, or accuracy-versus-COVID-outcome numbers are reported because the system does not perform automated diagnosis. CONFIDENCE: I could not open the full text, so any quantitative signal-comparison figures (e.g. agreement between camera PPG and reference) are not confirmed.
limitations: It is a proof-of-concept/prototype without a clinical validation trial, so real-world diagnostic or triage performance is unproven. No large labelled dataset and no trained diagnostic model — cough/respiration audio is only recorded, not automatically classified, and symptom-vs-vitals fusion relies on a human clinician. Phone-camera SpO2 is not established to clinical grade (reliable SpO2 needs the add-on device or a real oximeter read by OCR). App confirmed only on Android (Flutter); iOS not demonstrated. Follow-up literature notes the system lacked health-data interoperability standards (e.g. FHIR). Dependence on patient self-measurement raises data-quality/adherence concerns, and full source code for the complete system does not appear to be openly released (only the camera-PPG module is).
clinicalProblem: During COVID-19 surges, large numbers of patients with mild or moderate disease were isolated at home and monitored by health services mainly through repeated telephone calls. That approach is labour-intensive, gives clinicians only subjective verbal reports (no measured vital signs), and can miss the "silent" deterioration — especially falling blood-oxygen — that signals a patient needs hospital care. The target users are home-isolated / community-managed COVID-19 patients and the nurses and doctors tracking them. The problem this addresses is remote, scalable, objective monitoring and triage: giving each patient an easy way to self-measure fever, blood-oxygen, heart rate, cough/breathing and symptoms, and feeding that to a dashboard so clinicians can watch many patients and flag the ones getting worse. This matters because early detection of hypoxia and worsening symptoms can be the difference between timely treatment and a preventable bad outcome.
glossary: mHealth: healthcare delivered via mobile phones/apps. SpO2: percentage of haemoglobin in the blood carrying oxygen; low values signal respiratory trouble. PPG (photoplethysmography): an optical way to see the pulse by measuring light changes as blood pulses through tissue. Pulse oximeter: device that shines red/infrared light through a fingertip to estimate SpO2 and heart rate. MAX30101: a chip-sized optical pulse-oximeter/heart-rate sensor. MAX32664: a small "sensor hub" chip that runs the algorithm turning raw light signals into SpO2/heart-rate numbers. MLX90614: a non-contact infrared thermometer chip. ESP32: a cheap low-power microcontroller with built-in Wi-Fi/Bluetooth. Flutter: a toolkit for building phone apps that run from one codebase. OCR: optical character recognition — software that reads text/numbers from an image. Tympanic: relating to the eardrum/inner ear. FHIR: a standard format for exchanging health data between systems.

fullCitation: Joseph JW, Leventhal EL, Grossestreuer AV, Wong ML, Joseph LJ, Nathanson LA, Donnino MW, Elhadad N, Sanchez LD. Deep-learning approaches to identify critically ill patients at emergency department triage using limited information. Journal of the American College of Emergency Physicians Open (JACEP Open). 2020 Oct;1(5):773-781. doi:10.1002/emp2.12218. PMID 33145518; PMCID PMC7593422.
laySummary: When a patient arrives at an emergency department (ED), a triage nurse quickly records a few vital signs (like heart rate and blood pressure) and types a short free-text note of the patient's main complaint (e.g., "chest pain, short of breath"). This study asked whether a computer program could read just that small amount of information and flag patients likely to become critically ill (die or need intensive care within 24 hours). The researchers trained an artificial neural network on about 446,000 past ED visits and found that combining the typed complaint text with the numeric vital signs predicted critical illness far better than the standard triage tools nurses use today. The key idea is "fusion": teaching one model to blend the meaning of words with numbers. No new device or sensor is involved; the gain comes entirely from smarter software.
dataset: Name/source: a private, single-institution ED registry (not a public benchmark). Size: 445,925 adult ED visits screened, of which 60,901 (13.7%) met the critical-illness outcome. Population: adult patients at one academic, urban, tertiary-care emergency department in the Northeastern United States with an annual volume of roughly 55,000 visits. Time period: all visits between 1 January 2012 and 1 January 2020. Design: retrospective, observational, cross-sectional cohort using routinely collected, de-identified triage data. Prediction target/labels: a binary label of "critically ill," defined as in-hospital mortality OR admission to an intensive care unit within 24 hours of arrival; labels were derived from the hospital's electronic health record outcome data rather than manual chart review. Train/test split: the exact split was not stated in the text retrieved; performance is reported with tight 95% confidence intervals consistent with internal validation (likely cross-validation or bootstrap), but the precise partitioning is unconfirmed. Data is private/institutional; a de-identified subset with normalized vitals was posted to the code repository, and a version including chief-complaint text was pending institutional approval.
device: No physical device, sensor, phone, or add-on hardware is used or required. This is a pure software/machine-learning study: the innovation is the ALGORITHM that fuses free-text chief-complaint data with the numeric vital signs already collected during routine triage. Because there is no hardware, there is no phone-model dependency, no app to install for patients, and no per-unit cost — it would run as software inside a hospital's existing electronic health record or triage system. Cost of hardware: not applicable (well under any NT$5000 threshold since nothing must be bought). A dedicated app is NOT required. The code IS open source: the model code ("skeleton code for predicting critically ill patients from ED triage") is published as Jupyter notebooks under the MIT License at https://github.com/jwjoseph/NN_triage_predict . The specific deep-learning framework (e.g., Keras/TensorFlow) is not explicitly named in the retrieved README, so treat the framework as unconfirmed.
vitalsAndSensing: This paper introduces no new sensing technology; the physiological signs are the ordinary vital signs a triage nurse measures with standard clinical equipment, then typed or auto-imported into the record. Signs used (the "structured" inputs): heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure, temperature, and oxygen saturation (SpO2), plus age and sex as demographic context. Sensing mechanisms in plain terms: heart rate and SpO2 come from a fingertip pulse oximeter (a clip that shines light through the finger and reads how much is absorbed to estimate pulse and blood-oxygen level); blood pressure from an inflatable arm cuff; temperature from a digital thermometer; respiratory rate by counting breaths. The scientific contribution is NOT how these are measured but how their NUMBERS are combined, by the neural network, with the MEANING of the free-text complaint. Note: the paper describes the set as "initial vital signs"; the exact list above reflects standard ED triage vitals and the precise fields should be treated as representative rather than verbatim from the retrieved text.
chiefComplaintUse: The chief complaint is the centerpiece of this study. It is captured as the free-text note the triage nurse types describing why the patient came in (e.g., "weakness," "chest pain," "difficulty breathing"). Rather than forcing it into a fixed checklist, the model treats it as natural language: the words are tokenized and converted into numeric "word embeddings" (each word becomes a vector of numbers so that words with similar clinical meaning sit near each other), and these are fed into the neural network alongside the numeric vital signs. This lets the network learn, from data, which phrases signal danger. The study's headline result is precisely this fusion: adding the free-text chief complaint to the structured vitals raised discrimination from AUC ~0.82 (best structured-only model) to AUC 0.851, and hugely outperformed traditional triage rules such as abnormal-vital-sign triggers (AUC 0.521) and Emergency Severity Index (ESI) categories (AUC 0.672). The authors did not rely on a manual danger-sign checklist; the "danger signs" are learned implicitly from the text plus vitals.
pipelineStepLabels: Normalize vitals, age, sex to numbers
pipelineDetail: Patient arrives at ED triage: a person presents to the emergency department and is seen by a triage nurse for initial assessment. Nurse records vitals + free-text complaint: standard vital signs are measured and the nurse types a short free-text chief complaint into the record. Encode complaint as word embeddings: each word of the complaint is turned into a vector of numbers (an embedding) so the model can read meaning, not just characters. Normalize vitals, age, sex to numbers: the numeric inputs are scaled to comparable ranges so no single value dominates. Neural network fuses text + numbers: a trained multilayer neural network combines the embedded text with the numeric features in shared layers. Output critical-illness probability: the network's final unit produces a 0-to-1 probability that this patient will die or need ICU care within 24 hours. Threshold into high-risk flag / acuity: that probability is compared to a cutoff to raise a high-risk alert or sharpen the triage acuity assignment.
submodules: (1) Word-embedding encoder — role: convert free-text chief-complaint words into numeric vectors capturing clinical meaning; algorithm: learned word embeddings feeding the neural network (an embedding layer/representation trained on the study's own chief-complaint corpus); trained on the ~446k triage notes; input = tokenized complaint text, output = dense numeric vectors. (2) Combined (textual) neural network — the primary model; role: fuse text embeddings with structured vitals/age/sex and output critical-illness probability; algorithm: feedforward artificial neural network with a sigmoid output; trained by supervised learning on 445,925 visits with the binary 24-hour death/ICU label; input = embeddings + normalized numbers, output = probability. (3) Structured-only neural network — a 2-layer dense network using only vitals/age/sex (no text), serving as the ablation baseline (AUC 0.811). (4) Gradient tree boosting model — a boosted decision-tree model on the structured features used as a strong non-neural comparator (AUC 0.820). (5) Logistic regression — a simple linear baseline on structured features (AUC 0.803). Exact hidden-layer sizes, activation functions, and whether the text path used a recurrent/LSTM layer versus averaged embeddings are not confirmed in the retrieved text and should be verified in the code repository.
keyResults: Discrimination (AUC, the probability the model ranks a truly critically-ill patient above a well one; 1.0 = perfect, 0.5 = coin flip): best model = neural network WITH the free-text chief complaint added to vitals, AUC 0.851 (95% CI 0.849-0.852). Structured-data-only models: 2-layer neural network AUC 0.811 (95% CI 0.807-0.815), gradient tree boosting AUC 0.820 (95% CI 0.818-0.821), logistic regression AUC 0.803. Traditional triage tools were far weaker: abnormal-vital-sign trigger AUC 0.521 (barely better than chance) and ESI-based rule AUC 0.672. Takeaway in plain terms: adding the typed complaint text lifted performance by roughly 3+ AUC points over the best numbers-only model and dramatically beat the rule-based tools clinicians use today. (Some secondary summaries cite the textual model at AUC ~0.857; the value with a reported confidence interval is 0.851, which I treat as primary.)
limitations: Single-center, retrospective data from one US academic ED, so the model may not transfer to other hospitals, populations, or triage-documentation styles (external validation not done). The outcome (death or ICU admission within 24 hours) is a proxy for "critical illness" and can be influenced by local admission practices, so labels are imperfect. Free-text chief complaints vary by nurse, abbreviation, and typo, which can degrade the text model elsewhere. The study shows better prediction but does NOT demonstrate improved patient outcomes, workflow, or operational benefit — the authors explicitly note further research is needed to show clinical value. Class imbalance (only 13.7% positive) means AUC alone can overstate usefulness; sensitivity/specificity at a chosen operating threshold were not clearly surfaced in the retrieved text. Interpretability of the neural network is limited (a "black box" concern for clinicians). Exact model architecture and train/test methodology were not fully specified in the retrieved text.
glossary: Triage: rapid initial sorting of ED patients by how sick they are. Chief complaint: the short free-text reason a patient gives for coming to the ED. Critical illness (here): death or ICU admission within 24 hours of arrival. Vital signs: routine body measurements (heart rate, blood pressure, breathing rate, temperature, oxygen level). ESI (Emergency Severity Index): the standard 5-level triage acuity scale used by US nurses. Neural network: a layered software model loosely inspired by brain neurons that learns patterns from data. Deep learning: machine learning using multi-layer neural networks. Word embedding: turning each word into a list of numbers so similar-meaning words are numerically close, letting a model "read" text. AUC (AUROC): a 0.5-to-1.0 score for how well a model separates the two outcome groups; higher is better. Gradient tree boosting: a strong machine-learning method that combines many small decision trees. Logistic regression: a simple statistical model for yes/no prediction. Retrospective: using already-collected past records rather than enrolling new patients.
clinicalProblem: Emergency departments must decide within seconds-to-minutes, using very little information, which arriving patients are about to become critically ill. The standard tools — checking for abnormal vital signs or assigning an ESI level — miss many at-risk patients and are subjective. Under-triage delays life-saving care; over-triage wastes scarce resources. The patients here are all adults arriving at a busy US academic ED. Getting this front-door decision right, using only what is truly available at triage (a few vitals plus a typed complaint), directly affects who gets rapid attention and who deteriorates while waiting.
citationCount: ~30 citations (Semantic Scholar, as surfaced July 2026). Google Scholar was not directly reachable and typically reports a higher count; treat 30 as a Semantic Scholar lower bound.
impactFactor: Journal of the American College of Emergency Physicians Open (JACEP Open). JCR Journal Impact Factor 1.7 (2024); the journal earned its first Impact Factor of 2.3 (reported 2023). A specific CiteScore value was not confirmed. Note the article itself was published in 2020, before the journal had an Impact Factor.
confidenceNotes: Could not open the publisher/PMC/medRxiv full text directly (bot 403s and egress policy blocks); details were assembled from the abstract and multiple search-surfaced summaries plus the GitHub README, not verbatim from the full methods section. UNCONFIRMED items: (1) exact text-encoding method — whether learned embeddings were averaged/bag-of-embeddings or fed through a recurrent/LSTM layer, and embedding dimensionality; (2) exact neural-network architecture (hidden-layer count/sizes, activations) and the deep-learning framework; (3) precise train/validation/test split or cross-validation scheme; (4) the exact verbatim list of vital-sign fields (listed set reflects standard ED triage vitals); (5) reported sensitivity/specificity at an operating threshold; (6) whether the primary textual-model AUC is 0.851 (has a CI) versus 0.857 (appears in some secondary summaries) — I used 0.851 as primary. Citation count (~30) is from Semantic Scholar and is a snapshot lower bound. Author list confirmed via Semantic Scholar (Joseph, Leventhal, Grossestreuer, Wong, L.J. Joseph, Nathanson, Donnino, Elhadad, Sanchez).
sensors: This study uses no novel sensors. The physiological inputs come from standard, off-the-shelf clinical instruments already present at ED triage: a fingertip pulse oximeter (light-through-finger measurement of pulse and blood-oxygen saturation), an inflatable arm blood-pressure cuff, a digital thermometer, and manual/monitor counting of respiratory rate. The paper's "sensing" is really data capture: the nurse enters these numbers and types the chief complaint into the electronic record. All measurement is conventional; the научная novelty lives entirely in the software that fuses these numbers with the free-text.

fullCitation: Hoffman JS, Viswanath VK, Tian C, Ding X, Thompson MJ, Larson EC, Patel SN, Wang EJ. Smartphone camera oximetry in an induced hypoxemia study. npj Digital Medicine. 2022 Sep 19;5(1):146. doi:10.1038/s41746-022-00665-y. (University of Washington UbiComp Lab / UC San Diego. Preprint: arXiv:2104.00038.)
laySummary: Your blood needs enough oxygen; when it drops too low (a condition called hypoxemia) it warns of dangerous trouble in diseases like COVID-19, asthma and COPD. Doctors normally measure blood oxygen (SpO2) with a dedicated fingertip clip called a pulse oximeter. This study asked whether an ordinary, unmodified smartphone could do the same job: you press a fingertip over the phone's rear camera with the flash turned on, and software reads the tiny color flickers of your blood to estimate oxygen. To test it fairly, six volunteers safely breathed low-oxygen gas mixtures in a clinic so their real oxygen fell all the way to around 70 percent, and a computer model (a neural network) learned to predict those values. The phone method was off by about 5 percentage points on average and correctly flagged roughly 8 out of 10 dangerously low readings, which is promising but still less accurate than a real medical oximeter.
clinicalProblem: Hypoxemia (low blood-oxygen saturation, SpO2) is an early warning sign of deterioration in respiratory illnesses such as COVID-19, asthma, COPD and pneumonia. Standard-of-care pulse oximeters (the finger clip) are accurate but are a separate device many people do not own, especially in low-resource settings. If an ordinary smartphone could measure SpO2 through a simple software update, billions of people would gain a cheap, always-available screening tool for spotting when their oxygen is dropping to dangerous levels. The patients here were healthy adult volunteers used to build and validate the method, not sick patients — the paper is a proof-of-concept clinical validation, not a deployment trial.
dataset: Six healthy adult volunteers (subject IDs 10001-10006) participated in a controlled "varied fraction of inspired oxygen" (varied FiO2) induced-hypoxemia study run at Clinimark, an accredited clinical validation laboratory. Each participant reclined and breathed medically controlled oxygen-nitrogen gas mixtures for roughly 13-19 minutes, stepping their blood oxygen downward in stages to induce hypoxemia safely. This drove SpO2 across a wide, clinically relevant range of about 70-100 percent (individual readings spanned roughly 61-100 percent) — broader than prior smartphone studies that only reached 85-100 percent. More than 10,000 paired blood-oxygen readings were collected. Ground-truth SpO2 came from purpose-built, FDA-cleared reference (transmittance) pulse oximeters — the released dataset stores readings from four standard pulse oximeters logged at 1 Hz, alongside heart rate, perfusion index and oxygen-delivery values. The smartphone camera signal (per-frame averaged red, green, blue values) was logged at 30 Hz. Evaluation used a leave-one-subject-out scheme: the model was trained on the other subjects and tested on a held-out new subject, so reported accuracy reflects a person the model never saw. The dataset is public and open source (MIT license) on GitHub (ubicomplab/oximetry-phone-cam-data).
device: An UNMODIFIED consumer smartphone — a Google Nexus 6P — was used, with no clip, no add-on optics and no special sensor: the participant simply rests a fingertip over the rear camera while the built-in flash (LED torch) stays on. Video was captured at 30 frames per second by a custom data-collection app written in Java with Android Studio; the app fixed the camera color gains (red 1x, green 3x, blue 18x) so the dim blue/green light through the finger was usable. In principle any modern phone with a rear camera and flash could run the method via software, but the model was trained and validated on this single phone model, so cross-phone generalization is unproven. A dedicated app is required for capture, but no consumer app-store product was released. The dataset AND example analysis code (Python Jupyter notebooks) are OPEN SOURCE under the MIT license at https://github.com/ubicomplab/oximetry-phone-cam-data ; the technology is also listed for licensing via UW CoMotion. Cost: essentially zero beyond a phone people already own — well under NT$5000 (~US$155).
vitalsAndSensing: SpO2 (blood-oxygen saturation): fingertip covers the rear camera with the flash ON. The flash light passes into the finger and is partly absorbed by blood; the camera films the fingertip and records tiny rhythmic color changes as each heartbeat pushes blood through (this pulsating light signal is a photoplethysmogram, PPG). Oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor hemoglobin absorb red versus blue/green light by different amounts, so the ratio of the pulsating (AC) to steady (DC) components across color channels — the classic "ratio of ratios" — encodes oxygen saturation. A neural network converts these color-channel pulse signals into an SpO2 percentage. Heart rate is also implicitly present in the PPG (the pulse frequency), and the reference dataset additionally logs heart rate and perfusion index from the ground-truth oximeters.
chiefComplaintUse: No symptoms, chief complaint, questionnaire or danger-sign checklist are used. This is a pure physiological-signal study: the only inputs are the smartphone camera PPG signals, and the only output is estimated SpO2, which is then thresholded to flag hypoxemia (SpO2 below 90 percent). Clinical symptoms are mentioned only as motivation, not as model inputs.
pipelineDetail: Fingertip on camera + flash: the user presses a finger over the rear camera while the flash illuminates the tissue from within. Record RGB video (30 Hz): a custom app films the fingertip at 30 frames per second with fixed color gains so faint blue/green light is captured. Extract R/G/B pulse signals: each video frame is averaged into red, green and blue values over time, producing three pulsating waveforms (PPG). Filter & normalize PPG: the waveforms are cleaned of drift and noise and separated into their pulsating (AC) and steady (DC) parts. Ratio-of-ratios features: the AC/DC ratios across color channels are combined into the classic oximetry "ratio of ratios," the physical quantity that tracks oxygen. CNN SpO2 regression: a convolutional neural network, designed to mirror the ratio-of-ratios physics while suppressing heartbeat variability and camera noise, maps the signals to an oxygen estimate. SpO2 estimate: the model outputs a predicted blood-oxygen percentage for the held-out person. Threshold at 90% → hypoxemia flag: predictions below 90 percent are classified as hypoxemia, yielding a screening alert.
submodules: CNN SpO2 estimator: the single trained component. It is a convolutional neural network deliberately architected to replicate the mathematics of a conventional pulse oximeter (ratio-of-ratios) while (a) reducing the influence of beat-to-beat heartbeat variability and (b) handling the noise inherent to smartphone-camera PPG. Inputs: the processed red/green/blue camera PPG signals from a finger-on-camera clip. Output: a continuous SpO2 estimate. It was trained on the labeled color-signal-to-SpO2 pairs from the induced-hypoxemia dataset, with ground-truth labels from FDA-cleared reference pulse oximeters, and evaluated leave-one-subject-out (trained on the other five subjects, tested on the sixth). The ratio-of-ratios feature computation itself is an analytical signal-processing step, not a trained model; the paper and repo also note simpler analytical/linear-regression baselines as comparison approaches.
keyResults: On a held-out new subject (leave-one-subject-out), the deep-learning model estimated SpO2 with an overall mean absolute error (MAE) of 5.00 percent (standard deviation σ = 1.90) across the clinically relevant 70-100 percent range. For detecting hypoxemia, defined as SpO2 below 90 percent, the method reached about 81 percent sensitivity (correctly catching true low-oxygen cases) and 79 percent specificity (correctly clearing normal-oxygen cases). In plain terms: on average the phone's reading was within roughly 5 points of the true value, and it flagged about 8 of 10 dangerously low readings. For context, the FDA recommends cleared reflectance pulse oximeters achieve under 3.5 percent error across 70-100 percent, so this smartphone method is promising but not yet at medical-device accuracy.
limitations: Very small sample (only 6 healthy volunteers), so results may not generalize to real patients, older adults, or people with disease. A single phone model (Google Nexus 6P) was used, leaving cross-device generalization untested. The 5.00 percent MAE exceeds the FDA's <3.5 percent accuracy recommendation, so it is a screening/proof-of-concept, not a diagnostic-grade replacement. Skin-tone diversity was limited, a known and important source of pulse-oximetry bias that the study could not adequately assess. Data were collected under controlled, motionless laboratory conditions; real-world motion, ambient light, and finger-placement variability were not stress-tested. A custom capture app was needed and no validated consumer product was released.
glossary: SpO2: percentage of hemoglobin in the blood that is carrying oxygen; normal is ~95-100%. Hypoxemia: dangerously low blood oxygen, commonly flagged below 90%. Pulse oximeter: the finger-clip device that measures SpO2 with light. PPG (photoplethysmography): a light-based signal capturing the pulsating change in blood volume with each heartbeat. Ratio of ratios: the standard oximetry calculation comparing pulsating vs steady light absorption across two colors to infer oxygen. FiO2: the fraction of inspired oxygen in the air someone breathes; lowering it safely induces hypoxemia. Induced hypoxemia study: a controlled experiment that gently lowers a volunteer's blood oxygen to test a device across a wide range. CNN (convolutional neural network): a machine-learning model that learns patterns from signals or images. MAE (mean absolute error): average size of prediction error, in the same units (here percentage points of SpO2). Sensitivity: share of truly abnormal cases the test catches. Specificity: share of truly normal cases the test correctly clears. AC/DC components: the pulsating (AC) and steady (DC) parts of a light signal. Co-oximeter/reference oximeter: the accurate ground-truth device used as the gold standard.

sensors: Rear smartphone camera (a standard CMOS image sensor): with a fingertip pressed over it and the phone's LED flash lighting the tissue, the camera acts as a reflectance light sensor. Frame by frame it measures how much red, green and blue light returns from the blood-perfused finger. Because each heartbeat momentarily increases blood volume, the returning light dims and brightens rhythmically — the camera is effectively reading the pulse as a series of tiny color changes. The LED flash is the paired light source that makes this reflectance measurement possible. No other sensor, optic, or add-on hardware is involved.
